title: DNS: from a name to an address
summary: What happens between typing a name and connecting to an address: the chain of servers, the records, and why changes take time.

scheme: the resolver      in its cache? done
text: A program asks the C library for an address. It looks in /etc/hosts first, then asks a DNS resolver: your router's, your provider's, or one you chose.
- The order is set by the hosts: line of /etc/nsswitch.conf (usually files, then dns).
When the resolver doesn't know, it walks down from the root. Each server knows only the next step.
- The last one is authoritative: it holds the domain's records.
- The resolver keeps each answer in its cache: next time, no walk.
A domain holds records of different types.
- A CNAME says: this name is another name, ask for that one.
- PTR goes backwards, from an address to a name (dig -x).
Every answer comes with a TTL: how long resolvers may keep it.
- Change a record, and caches keep the old answer until their copy expires.
- Before a planned move, lower the TTL (300) a day ahead, move, then raise it again.
